title: Labelling a scene by looking at small patches and their neighbours
paper_title: Combining multilevel contexts of superpixel using convolutional neural networks to perform natural scene labeling
date_note: Springer AISC vol. 740 (IC3 2018 proceedings) went online 11 Sep 2018; the PDF gives no conference dates and I could not confirm them, so the online publication date is used
venue: Recent Developments in Machine Learning and Data Analytics (IC3)
authors: A Das, Swarnendu Ghosh, R Sarkhel, S Choudhuri, N Das, M Nasipuri
summary: We label outdoor scenes by classifying superpixels (small patches of similar pixels) with their neighbours. Three small networks combined reached 77.14% accuracy on ICCV09, in 25 to 30 ms of testing time.

body.p: Scene labelling means giving every part of a photo a name such as sky, tree, grass or road. Most deep-learning methods do this one pixel at a time, and a single pixel says very little about what it belongs to. We worked with superpixels instead, and gave each one a look at its neighbours. Three small networks each classified every patch, and a merging step combined their answers into a result that compares well with other published methods on the same dataset.

A superpixel is a small patch of neighbouring pixels that look alike and are grouped together. An image ends up with far fewer patches than pixels. We used an algorithm called SLIC to cut each image up, because it is fast and its patches follow object edges well.

The number of patches is set by a quantity we call the minimum object resolution. We fixed it at roughly 20×20 pixels. Over the whole dataset this gave 291,911 superpixels. Classifying a patch is much cheaper than classifying every pixel, and a patch shows texture, which a single pixel cannot.

A patch on its own can still be ambiguous, because similar-looking patches can belong to different classes. What surrounds the patch carries extra information. So for each superpixel we built three inputs. The first is the patch alone. The second adds its immediate neighbours, and the third adds the neighbours of those neighbours.

figure.alt: Left: a photo of trees cut into superpixels with a small red outline on one patch and two nested red boxes labelled 1N and 2N around it. Right, top row: that patch alone, with its first ring of neighbours, and with its second ring. Bottom row: the patch outline, its bounding box, and an empty regular-sized box.
figure.caption: One superpixel (red) is cut out alone (b), then with its first neighbours (c) and with its second neighbours (d). The bottom row shows how a cut-out is put into a regular-sized box before it goes into a network.

body.p: We trained a separate convolutional neural network for each of the three inputs. A convolutional network is a stack of small learned filters that pick out patterns in an image. Ours were deliberately small: two layers of filters, one fully connected layer of 256 units, and an output that gives a probability for each of the 8 classes. The input sizes were 24×24, 32×32 and 48×48 pixels, chosen by performance on validation images.

figure.alt: Flowchart. An image is split into superpixels by SLIC. Three inputs (patch alone, patch plus first neighbours, patch plus second neighbours) go through three separate small convolutional networks, whose outputs feed one ensemble step: max-voting, weighted voting or Dempster-Shafer theory.
figure.caption: The whole pipeline. Three networks see the same patch at three levels of context, and an ensemble step merges their answers.

body.p: We tried three ways of merging. Max-voting takes the class that most networks choose. A weighted average blends the probabilities, trusting each network according to how well it did in training. The third uses the Dempster-Shafer theory of evidence. Instead of one probability per class, it deals with belief spread over groups of classes. We estimated this from the confusion matrix, the table of which classes a network mixed up during training, so that a patch can carry some belief for a class that is often confused with its top choice.

We used the ICCV09 dataset: 715 photos with 8 classes, split into 500 for training, 72 for validation and 143 for testing. The three networks alone scored almost the same: 72.32% for the patch alone, 72.45% with first neighbours and 72.24% with second neighbours (Table 1). From that you might think the neighbours add nothing. Combining them showed otherwise.

body.callout: The weighted average of the three networks reached 77.14% accuracy on the ICCV09 test images, against about 72% for each network alone (Table 1, Table 2).

body.p: Dempster-Shafer gave 77.07% and max-voting 72.88% (Table 2). The weighted average and Dempster-Shafer were close, and each came out ahead on some classes. On this dataset our result of 77.14% was above the pixel-based CRF baseline (74.3%), the CNN plus superpixel method of Farabet et al. (74.56%) and three other published methods (76.3% to 76.9%) (Table 3). Testing took 25 to 30 milliseconds on a GTX 1080 graphics card, which the paper takes as enough for real-time use.

figure.alt: Six photos of roads, trees, buildings and a motorbike rider, each next to its coloured label map, with a colour key for sky, foreground object, grass, tree, road, building, water and mountain.
figure.caption: Example outputs. Large regions such as sky, trees and road are labelled in clear blocks, and the outlines follow the superpixels.

body.p: The mountain class almost failed: accuracy was 2.56% with Dempster-Shafer and about 4% with the other two methods (Table 2). Segments with mountains are scarce in the dataset, so the networks had little to learn from. Water and foreground objects were also weaker than sky or ground (Table 2). We tested only on ICCV09.
We saw video segmentation as the natural next step, since a fast method built on relatively small networks suits it.
